sentences.text: Cardabiodon possessed a very heavy and stocky body structure with a rigid, spindle-shaped vertebral column that was poorly flexible but efficient for fast swimming. Its skin was covered in teardrop-shaped scales with 6 to 8 parallel grooves and kneels, a unique dental structure unlike any other known living or extinct shark. In this shark, lower jaw tooth size abruptly increased to peak at the first lateroposterior tooth, contrary to the gradual decrease seen in other mackerel sharks.
Reconstructions of vertebrae and jaws suggest Cardabiodon reached a maximum size of 5.5 meters.
An early Cardabiodontid individual from the Albian age was estimated to reach a length of 8 to 9 meters.
The Carlile Shale near Mosby, Montana, has been identified as a nursery area for Cardabiodon due to the high prevalence of juvenile fossils.
The genus Cardabiodon was named by Mikael Siverson in 1999, and the type species of the genus is Cardabiodon ricki.
The second species, C. venator, was described in 2005 by Siverson and Johan Lindgren based on 37 teeth found in Montana.

Cardabiodon was likely an apex predator that hunted plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs, and large fish using its robust teeth and fast swimming. As a presumed apex predator, Cardabiodon likely preyed on various marine vertebrates coexisting in the Western Interior Seaway, including sharks, bony fish, seabirds, marine reptiles, and sea turtles.
The specialized scales of Cardabiodon suggest it was capable of fast swimming to pursue lively prey.

Vertebrae of Cardabiodon ricki suggest that newborn individuals were between 41 and 76 cm in total length, which is smaller than the birth sizes of Cretoxyrhina mantelli and Archaeolamna kopingensis. Three vertebral specimens of Cardabiodon ricki showed thirteen growth rings, indicating these individuals lived to approximately 13 years of age.

Most Cardabiodon fossils come from North America, specifically the southern half of the Western Interior Seaway. Like modern sharks, Cardabiodon utilized shallow nursery areas to protect its young from predators.

Research suggests Cardabiodon shifted its distribution farther north before the Cenomanian-Turonian Thermal Optimum (about 93 Ma) due to rising temperatures. It is proposed that Cardabiodon could migrate between hemispheres by crossing deeper, cooler waters. The hypothesis of inter-hemispheric migration is supported by the presence of Cardabiodon teeth in deep-water deposits near its lowest paleolatitude range.

Cardabiodon lived during the Cenomanian-Turonian Thermal Optimum, a time of significant biodiversity change and the radiation of new fauna like mosasaurs. Benthic fauna was rare in the northern waters inhabited by Cardabiodon due to low oxygen levels from the Cenomanian-Turonian anoxic event, which caused the extinction of up to 27% of marine invertebrates.

Cardabiodon belongs to the unique family Cardabiodontidae and includes the species C. ricki and C. venator. Siverson established the family Cardabiodontidae to include Cardabiodon and the extinct Cenozoic shark Parotodus due to their unique dental structures. The Late Cretaceous shark Dwardius, which has teeth very similar to Cardabiodon, is also placed within the family Cardabiodontidae.

Cardabiodon lived between 95 and 91 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous. Fossils of an early Cardabiodontid, including teeth and vertebrae, date to the Albian age (105 million years ago) and were found in the Toolebuc Formation in Queensland. Cardabiodon lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Cenomanian and Turonian stages, approximately 99.7 to 94.3 million years ago.
Cardabiodon inhabited sea surface temperatures ranging from 17.5 to 24.2 degrees Celsius.

Siverson concluded that the former taxon Cretolamna woodwardi likely represents two distinct genera, one of which is Cardabiodon. A 2010 study led by Todd D. Cook proposed that Cardabiodon and Dwardius might be synonymous genera, though Siverson expressed unlikeliness due to contradictory evolutionary trends.
